profiles.meeting_scenario: EvaSylv is being reviewed as a near-beta decision-support product for forestry consulting firms and cooperative forest managers. The meeting is a design review of the current product proposal for the first external pilot: the team is evaluating whether the workflow, outputs, and sample content are sufficiently complete for a limited release of the stand-level scenario simulator covering thinning schedules, cutting age, and optional natural-risk modeling. The agenda is to review the pilot experience from scenario setup through results interpretation, check whether the current design meets pilot expectations for non-programmer users, and decide what modifications are needed before approval. The expected outcome is a go/no-go recommendation for the external pilot plus a short list of design changes.

members.name: Claire Dubois
members.expertise: B2B analytics products, pilot launches, packaging technical tools for consultant workflows
members.background: Claire has spent eight years launching decision-support software for environmental and infrastructure clients and now leads productization for EvaSylv's commercial pilot.
members.private_state: Claire wants the pilot approved this month because two forestry cooperatives are waiting for a demoable version, and she is comfortable compensating for rough edges with onboarding calls and analyst support as long as the product appears coherent and usable in client-facing sessions.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the product needs a 'default scenario,' they mean a preloaded demonstration setup that lets a pilot user open the tool and see plausible outputs immediately.
A design is 'ready for pilot' if invited users can complete a guided evaluation with light manual support from the team; full self-service is not required yet.
The 'export' expected in the pilot is a polished summary artifact for discussion with landowners or cooperative clients, not a full methodological audit package.
The pine carbon case study has already moved from internal illustration to approved external demo content because it has been shown in prior sponsor updates.

members.name: Julien Morel
members.role: UX Lead and Forestry Workflow Specialist
members.expertise: Decision-support interfaces, forestry practitioner workflows, translating scientific models into operational tools
members.background: Julien previously worked with a regional forestry advisory network before moving into product design, and he now owns the user workflow and interpretability of EvaSylv for practitioners who are not programmers.
members.private_state: Julien wants to protect the credibility of the tool with practitioners and worries that a pilot released too early will create mistrust if users cannot understand assumptions, reproduce scenarios, or distinguish baseline and risk-adjusted outputs on their own.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'default scenario,' they mean the baseline comparator used inside the analysis, typically the unmanaged or no-risk reference against which management scenarios are interpreted.
A design is 'ready for pilot' only if a typical forestry consultant can navigate it without live guidance and still correctly interpret both economic and ecosystem-service outputs.
The necessary 'export' for this kind of tool must include parameters, assumptions, and scenario definitions so results can be traced and defended later.
The pine carbon case study is still an internal demonstration asset because external reuse depends on partner permission and clearer labeling of the embedded assumptions.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to adding or reviewing the 'default scenario' in the pilot flow.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire means the prefilled demo configuration that opens with sample values so users can quickly see a complete EvaSylv run during a first session.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien means the analytical baseline scenario inside the comparison view, namely the reference case against which managed and risk-adjusted scenarios are judged.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In product discussions, 'default scenario' sounds ordinary and helpful in either sense, and both meanings fit a simulator product, so each hears the phrase as confirming their own assumption without feeling any need to disambiguate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they want the build to be 'ready for pilot' after a few adjustments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire believes readiness means the current build is stable enough for a controlled pilot with invited users, guided onboarding, and some behind-the-scenes support from the product team.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien believes readiness means the workflow is independently understandable by practitioners, with enough clarity in setup and result interpretation that they do not need real-time hand-holding.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Teams often use 'pilot' as a shared milestone label, and because both support making some fixes before release, the conversation feels aligned even though their thresholds for sufficiency are materially different.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the pilot should include an 'export' so users can share results.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire assumes export means a concise PDF or slide-ready summary of stand assumptions and top outputs like Faustmann value, averaged yield, and risk/no-risk comparison charts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien assumes export includes the full scenario specification, model switches, and assumptions appendix so consultants can revisit, compare, and defend the run later.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Everyone expects software to have some form of export, and 'share results' naturally covers both presentation and documentation use cases, so the difference in boundaries stays invisible during a normal review.

misalignment_points.topic: Status of the pine carbon case study
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to using 'the pine carbon case' in the pilot materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Claire presupposes the pine stand carbon-sequestration example is already cleared for external pilot demos because it has been used in sponsor-facing updates and illustrates non-financial optimization well.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Julien presupposes the same case is still internal-only because the source assumptions and partner permissions were never formally packaged for outside users.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither person treats content clearance as an active topic in a design review; the case study feels like an already-known artifact, so each assumes shared history and moves on.

turns.inner_thought: I need a clear yes on the pilot this month if possible. The cooperatives do not need a fully autonomous product yet; they need something coherent enough to walk through in a live session and react to. If we can keep the experience smooth and control the first impression with onboarding, we can absolutely call this ready for pilot after a short polish pass.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. What I want to get to today is pretty simple: are we comfortable saying the current EvaSylv flow is ready for pilot, and if not, what are the last light adjustments before we send it to the two cooperative partners?

turns.inner_thought: The structure is much better than it was, but I still care less about whether we can demo it and more about whether a forestry consultant can open it alone and not misread the analysis. If people need us beside them to explain what they are looking at, it is not actually ready for pilot in the way that matters for credibility.
turns.utterance: Overall, I think the flow is stronger now. My main check is whether a first-time consultant can get through the setup and the comparisons without getting lost or drawing the wrong conclusion from the screens.

turns.inner_thought: The biggest win for the pilot would be opening straight into a complete example so nobody lands on an empty state. A prefilled beech run with outputs already visible makes the tool feel real immediately, and then we can guide them from there. That is what I mean by the default scenario being essential.
turns.utterance: For me, the landing experience clicks if the default scenario opens right away with a complete beech example and visible outputs, including the risk and no-risk views. That makes the first session much easier.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, the default scenario matters, but only if it is unmistakable in the comparison view as the reference case. Otherwise users won't know what the managed options are being judged against, and they may compare the wrong things. I assume Claire is talking about the same analytical anchor.
turns.utterance: I agree, the default scenario is important. I would just make sure it is very clearly identified in the comparison panel so people always know what the other scenarios are being measured against.

turns.inner_thought: We do not need a giant reporting engine for the pilot. What advisors need is something clean they can bring into a meeting with landowners or a cooperative contact: a tidy summary that looks credible and supports the discussion. If we overbuild here, we lose time we don't have.
turns.utterance: On outputs, I think the pilot just needs an export that lets advisors share results cleanly in a landowner conversation. If that piece is presentable, it covers the main use case for the first round.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, absolutely an export, but it has to preserve enough detail that someone can come back later and understand exactly what was run. In forestry advisory work, if the assumptions and scenario setup are not carried through, the result becomes hard to defend. I assume Claire sees that as part of 'share results.'
turns.utterance: Yes, and the export should make the scenario reusable later as well, so when users share results they're not losing the thread of how they got there. That will help a lot with confidence in the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: If the beech example is stable, the pilot deck will be much stronger with the pine carbon case too. It shows we're not only optimizing for timber economics, and we've already shown that case in sponsor updates, so I take it as fair game for external materials.
turns.utterance: If the beech flow is stable, I would also strengthen the pilot deck by using the pine carbon case as the second example. It gives us a nice way to show the ecosystem-service side without changing the core story.

turns.inner_thought: I like using the pine carbon case because it surfaces the assumptions in a way practitioners can discuss, though I still think of it as something we need to handle carefully before it goes outside. Still, as a design example, it is the right contrast to the economic one.
turns.utterance: I like that. The pine carbon case is useful because it makes the assumptions in that kind of run much easier to read than in the purely economic example.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're aligned enough to move. If we polish the opening experience, include the export, and package the beech and pine examples, I can confidently position this as ready for pilot and get the partner sessions scheduled. We can support any rough edges manually.
turns.utterance: So from my side, if we polish the default scenario, include the export, and finalize those two case-study examples, I see the build as essentially ready for pilot.

turns.inner_thought: I still want the guidance and result framing tightened before I am truly comfortable, but those are exactly the places to work. If I can sharpen the interpretation cues around the reference and comparison views, then users should be able to read the outputs correctly on their own, which is what ready for pilot means to me.
turns.utterance: Yes, that sounds like the right list. I'll refine the guidance and the result views so pilot users can interpret the baseline, the scenarios, and the outputs with confidence.
